title: Cache coalescing and spill strategy field notes
content:
Context and intent:

Quick notes capturing experiments and intuition around reducing page faults and read amplification by using small-window coalescing and smarter spill strategies for our KV cache. This doc is a working artifact — contains raw measurements, failed hypotheses, and suggested next steps. Goal: identify a low-complexity change we can A/B in canary to reduce sustained memory bandwidth and page-in overhead on 40B-class weights with long context.

Executive summary (TL;DR):
- Observed a correlated spike in paging stall time (major page-ins) when reuse drops below ~12% for long-form chat sessions (seq length > 2048).
- Simple coalescing of adjacent KV slots (coalescing window 4) reduced page-ins by ~20% and read-amplification by ~18% in synthetic replay tests, at <2% CPU overhead.
- Aggressive spill-to-disk (-spill-threshold low) hurts latency tail due to synchronous page-in on warmups; prefer spill-to-NUMA+background-prefetch approach.
- Recommendation: prototype a bandwidth-aware coalescing layer + background async spill reader and deploy to a small Dedicated pool for validation.

Benchmark and trace sources:
- Prod-like replay: trace-2024-10-22-serve-main (12h sample, mixed chat + singleton prompts).
- Microbenchmarks: seq-rand-access and seq-coherent-access harnesses in tools/kv-bench (commit 1a2f3b).
- Hardware: p4d-24xlarge equivalent nodes (A100-like), kernel 6.1.x, numa enabled.

Key observations (detailed):
1) Reuse cliff and paging spikes:
- When the measured per-request KV reuse rate falls below ~12% (definition: fraction of required KV entries found in local resident set before any read), the system started showing 30–120ms extra stall attributed to page-ins at the OS level (measured via perf::major-faults and bpftrace kv_page_in.c).
- These page-ins were concentrated in a small hotset of pages that were partially resident and frequently accessed across requests; fragmentation + allocator alignment pushed parts of the hotset to different physical pages.

2) Coalescing window experiment:
- Hypothesis: grouping logically adjacent KV entries into a single physical allocation reduces number of distinct pages touched per request.
- Implemented a proof-of-concept coalescer (coalesce_window=4) that packs 4 sequential KV blocks into one contiguous slab and aligns to 64KB boundaries to reduce page spread.
- Results (seq-coherent-access, 100k requests):
  * baseline page-ins/request: 0.85
  * coalescer(4) page-ins/request: 0.68 (20% reduction)
  * CPU overhead: +1.5% system CPU for slab management
  * tail latency (p99 gen): improved by ~6ms in this microbenchmark.
- Notes: diminishing returns beyond window~8 due to increased internal fragmentation and write amplification for evictions.

3) Bandwidth-aware eviction (bcLRU) prototype:
- Problem: classic LRU evicts entries evenly, but evicting a large contiguous block that maps to few physical pages can cause large immediate page-in bandwidth when reads resume.
- Implemented a heuristic: score = decay*recency + alpha*(pages_mapped_by_entry) + beta*(last_access_interval); prefer evicting high-score entries with low pages_mapped and high recency.
- Observed lower sustained memory bandwidth during load spikes: 12–15% reduction in read BW in replay tests; however, p95 latency sometimes increased due to slightly higher misses for some synthetic patterns.

4) Spill strategies and async prefetch:
- Spill-to-disk synchronous: causes large latency outliers on cold warmups. Avoid for latency-sensitive tiers.
- Spill-to-NUMA (move between local and remote node memory) + async prefetch worked best: when an entry is evicted from local node, schedule a low-priority background prefetch for predicted warm entries based on short-window reuse history (W=32).
- Implementation detail: use rdma/memcopy path with high NIC priority throttle; mark prefetches with cgroup nice so they yield to production traffic.

5) TLB / page coloring / allocator notes:
- On a few runs we saw TLB shootdowns and page coloring fragmentation exacerbating page spread. Suspect our jemalloc config + hugepage mix causes non-ideal color distribution for KV slabs.- Quick mitigation: force 2MB hugepage allocation for very large slabs (>2MB) and use 64KB alignment for smaller slabs to keep hotset compact.

Instrumentation & commands used:
- perf stat -e major-faults,minor-faults,cycles,cache-misses -a -- sleep 30
- bpftrace -e 'tracepoint:syscalls:sys_enter_mmap { @[comm] = count(); }' - note: used to capture mmap churn during coalescer testing.
- nvprof / nsys for GPU kernel overlaps with CPU prefetch threads (to ensure prefetch doesn't starve kernels).
- Custom counters exposed via runtime/telemetry: kv.resident_pct, kv.evicted_by_policy, kv.prefetch_attempts, kv.spill_count.

Raw numbers excerpt (representative):
- Baseline resident_pct (trace sample): 34%
- Coalescer(4) resident_pct: 37% (+3ppt)
- Baseline read BW (avg during spike): 145 GB/s
- bcLRU read BW: 128 GB/s (-12%)
- Major page faults baseline (per-minute, host): 420 -> after coalescer: 335

Microbench harness config (how to reproduce):
- tools/kv-bench --trace replay/trace-2024-10-22-serve-main --coalesce-window 4 --evict-policy bcLRU --prefetch async --duration 3600 --out results/ccs-20241107.log
- Note: set environment KV_ALLOC_ALIGN=65536 for slab alignment experiments.

Tradeoffs and failure modes:
- Coalescing increases internal fragmentation: for workloads dominated by tiny prompts with sparse KV access, memory overhead rises ~4–7% leading to slightly higher OOM risk under memory pressure.
- bcLRU relies on reasonably stable page-size mapping estimates; noisy access patterns can mislead pages_mapped computation and worsen p99 if tuning off.
- Background prefetch needs strong isolation — if it competes with foreground it can harm gen kernels. We mitigated with cgroup and NIC throttles in the prototype.

Open questions and experiments to run next:
- Run coalescer + bcLRU with real canary: small Dedicated pool (10 nodes) under prod routing policy for 48h to verify tail behavior.
- Investigate allocator changes: jemalloc arena pinning + page coloring to reduce interleaving between KV slabs and other runtime allocations. Does it reduce TLB churn?
- Explore hybrid hugepage strategy: 2MB for large slabs, 64KB for small — measure fragmentation vs page-in latency impact.
- Can we attach a short-term bloom filter per slab to avoid unnecessary async prefetch for entries unlikely to be re-requested? Measure cost of maintaining bloom metadata.

Action items / next steps:
- [Asha] Finalize microbench harness and add telemetry hooks for pages_mapped estimate and prefetch success rate. (ETA: 2024-11-18)
- [Miguel] Add jemalloc config toggles to the canary AMI and run memory stress suites. (ETA: 2024-11-22)
- [Liang] Implement simple adaptive prefetch throttle (PID-ish) that reduces prefetch rate when GPU kernel stall increases. (ETA: 2024-11-20)
- [Erin] Prepare canary rollout plan (10-node Dedicated, whitelist customers, observability dashboard) and coordinate with infra. (ETA: 2024-11-25)

Notes to reviewers:
- This was a quick field test; logs and raw perf captures are uploaded to S3 (see linked artifacts). Please look specifically at p99 gen tail under mixed random/coherent traces — that's where false positives for bcLRU showed up once.
- I'm intentionally conservative on default coalesce_window (start at 4). We can expose as a per-model config if initial canary shows good results.

References / previous work:
- See experiments: kv-coalescing-prototype branch and PR linked above.
- Related reading: internal notes on "kv-warmth-signatures" and prefetching heuristics (search Drive for warmth-signatures).

Appendix: quick glossary:
- resident_pct: fraction of KV entries present in local node memory before request servicing.
- coalescing window: number of logical KV entries packed per physical allocation.
- bcLRU: bandwidth-aware LRU scoring heuristic used here.
- pages_mapped: estimate of how many physical pages a logical KV entry touches (used in scoring).

-- end of notes --

(If you copy experiments, please update linked_artifacts with the run id and sample_id so we can track reproducibility.)
